newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ court overturns cutback of snapper quotas.
newsitem.headline: NZ court overturns cutback of snapper quotas.

text.p: Former fisheries minister Doug Kidd acted unlawfully when he cut back commercial snapper fishing on the East Coast of the North Island, the Court of Appeal said on Wednesday.

The New Zealand Press Association reported the court overturned a High Court decision that had ruled against the fishing industry and Maori interests who had sought a review of government plans to cut the annual commercial snapper catch by 40 percent.
The government had wanted quota cuts in the fishery, which extends from North Cape to East Cape, to ensure its survival.
Kidd, who is now Parliament's Speaker, had ordered the cuts for the 1995 fishing year, but interim court orders have so far prevented the cuts taking effect.
Delivering the Appeal Court's judgment, Justice Tipping said the minister had failed to consider a mandatory consideration in ordering the cut and had been wrongly advised of his legal obligations.
But the court also said Maori holders of quota were not protected from a cut if there was to be one.
Justice Tipping said the court agreed with the appellants that the minister had failed to consider -- as he was obliged to by law -- crown acquisition of quota as an alternative to making a cut.
This would involve the Crown retaining or obtaining the right to take fish under an appropriate quota and not making those rights available for commercial fishing.
"The minister's failure is related directly to what can be seen as an erroneous statement of the legal position in the advice which he received," Tipping said.
The appeal, heard from June 30 to July 3 this year, was brought by the Fishing Industry Association, the Treaty of Waitangi Fisheries Commission and other fishing and Maori fishing interests.
A High Court judge in April had turned down their challenge to the way the cuts were decided.
The Maori and general fishing industries have claimed the quota cut would cause widespread job losses, particularly in small communities in the north.
